title: Why master one language before jumping to another

videos.script:
You know JavaScript. This course takes it out of the page and puts it on a server. {{fork}} You chose this path at a fork in the track. Python, Java and Go were the other three. This lesson starts with why the advice is to stay with one of them until you know it well.

{{depth}} The short answer is that a language is not its syntax. It is a runtime, a way of finding code, a library, and a crowd of tools. Learning those twice, at the same time, means knowing neither.

{{wait}} Then what Node is good at. A server spends most of its time waiting for a database or a disk. Node waits without holding a thread, so one process can keep thousands of requests in the air. You will also see the one thing that breaks it.

{{setup}} After that, your computer. If you took the JavaScript course, Node 22 is already there, and you will only check that it answers. If not, the steps are here in brief.

{{server}} And then a first server, in a handful of lines, that answers a request from a second terminal. By the end you will have read your first stack trace, and know where the documentation for your version lives.
